title: India's Inflation Just Hit a New-Series High. For NRIs, the Real Number Is Much Worse.
excerpt: Official CPI rose to 3.93% in May, but food inflation is at 4.78%, fuel prices have been hiked four times, and the RBI just raised its full-year forecast to 5.1%. Every rupee you send home now buys less than it did in January.
body:
The number looks reassuring at first glance. India's retail inflation, measured by the Consumer Price Index, came in at 3.93% for May — comfortably below the Reserve Bank of India's 4% medium-term target and well within the 2-to-6% tolerance band. Crisis averted, one might think.

Look closer, and the picture is considerably less comfortable. For anyone sending money home to India — or holding rupee-denominated assets, or planning a trip back, or helping parents manage household budgets from abroad — the real story is in the components, not the headline.

## The Food Bill Is Rising Fast

Food inflation accelerated to 4.78% in May, up from 4.20% in April and 3.87% in March. That is three consecutive months of acceleration, and the trajectory matters more than any single print.

Within food, the distribution is savage. Tomato prices are up 48.4% year-on-year. Ginger is up 32.5%. Gold and silver jewellery — a staple of Indian household savings and wedding spending — has surged, with silver jewellery inflation at an extraordinary 155.2%.

The only meaningful deflation is in potatoes, which fell 23.7%, and peas, down 11.5%. These are welcome but cannot offset the broader trend.

Rural areas are being hit harder than cities. Rural food inflation stands at 4.85% versus 4.66% in urban areas. For NRI families whose parents and extended family live in smaller towns and villages — which is most of them — this gap matters directly.

## Four Fuel Hikes in One Month

State-owned fuel retailers raised petrol and diesel prices four times in May alone. The cumulative increase since the start of the month is 7.4% for petrol and 8.4% for diesel.

Transport inflation jumped to 1.75% in May from a 0.01% decline in April. This is the pass-through from the Middle East conflict — the Iran war and the effective blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have kept Brent crude above $87 per barrel, and India imports roughly 90% of its oil.

For Indian households, the effects of fuel price increases cascade through everything: auto-rickshaw fares, delivery charges, cooking gas, and the cost of transporting food from farm to market. The full inflationary impact of May's hikes has not yet worked through the system.

## The RBI Sees Worse Ahead

The central bank is not pretending this will pass quickly. In its June policy review, the RBI revised its inflation forecast for the full fiscal year 2026-27 upward to 5.1%, from 4.6% in the previous estimate. The quarterly breakdown is sobering: 4.2% in Q1 (April to June), 5.1% in Q2, 5.9% in Q3, and 5.4% in Q4.

That Q3 projection — 5.9% — is approaching the upper boundary of the RBI's tolerance band. If it materialises, it would constrain the central bank's ability to cut rates, even as growth projections are being marked down. The RBI's own growth forecast for FY27 now stands at 6.6%, with a downside risk of 20 to 30 basis points. Before the Iran conflict, the chief economic adviser had projected 7.0% to 7.4%.

Two forces are converging to push prices higher in the second half of the year. First, the fading base effect — inflation was unusually low in the comparable months of 2025, so year-on-year comparisons will mechanically rise. Second, the El Niño.

## The Monsoon Wildcard

The India Meteorological Department confirmed on June 12 that moderate-to-strong El Niño conditions are expected to prevail throughout the June-to-September monsoon season. The monsoon delivers nearly 70% of India's rainfall and is essential for agriculture, which accounts for about 18% of the economy.

El Niño years are historically associated with below-normal rainfall. The IMD has forecast total monsoon rainfall at 90% of the long-period average, with June expected to deliver just 92%. Below-normal monsoon rainfall would reduce output of rice, pulses, oilseeds, and cotton — crops that directly feed into food inflation and rural incomes.

The timing is particularly bad. The combination of elevated energy costs from the Iran conflict and potential crop shortfalls from El Niño creates what economists call overlapping supply shocks. Aberdeen Investments' Michael Langham put it bluntly: "India is set for a series of supply shocks," adding that the RBI's ability to look through the energy price shock will become "increasingly difficult."

## What This Means for NRIs

The practical implications run across several channels.

**Remittances buy less.** The rupee has depreciated over 5% year-to-date, meaning each dollar converts to more rupees. But if inflation erodes the purchasing power of those rupees faster than the exchange rate improves, the net benefit shrinks. A dollar sent home today buys more rupees but fewer tomatoes.

**Family budgets are under pressure.** For NRIs supporting parents, funding children's education in India, or maintaining property, the monthly cost of living is rising visibly. Cooking gas, vegetables, and transport are all moving higher simultaneously.

**Investment returns need reframing.** Nominal returns on Indian fixed deposits and bonds look attractive — bank FD rates of 7% or more, government bond yields near 6.9%. But with inflation heading toward 5% or higher, real returns are thinning. The RBI's decision not to hike rates — which some market participants had feared — suggests the central bank is still prioritising growth, but that calculus changes if inflation breaches 5.5%.

**Wedding and travel costs are elevated.** Gold and jewellery inflation above 40% means wedding budgets for anyone planning ceremonies in India need to be substantially revised upward from even six months ago.

The headline inflation number of 3.93% is the least informative figure in the release. The composition — food at 4.78%, fuel spiking, jewellery at triple digits, and the RBI projecting 5.9% by the autumn — paints a picture that requires active attention, not passive comfort.
nri_angle: NRI remittances are worth less in real terms as India's food and fuel inflation accelerates — the RBI's revised 5.1% forecast for FY27 means the purchasing power of every dollar sent home is eroding faster than at any point since the new CPI series launched.
author: Diaspora Desk
